body.text: When UDP demand is below its configured share, the scheduler gives the unused UDP share to TCP, so TCP goodput is nearly independent of weightUdp above the UDP-demand threshold.
body.question: Does lowering UDP share above UDP demand change TCP throughput?
body.why: It tells whether weightUdp can be reduced to help TCP without hurting UDP.
body.prediction: tcp_goodput_bps at weightUdp=0.35 is within 1% of the default weightUdp=0.50, and udp_loss_frac at weightUdp=0.35 is <=0.01.
body.observations: Default run r001 (weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, duration=10) gives udp_goodput_bps=300003200, tcp_goodput_bps=668633114, udp_loss_frac=0.0, drops_band0=0, drops_band1=92, tcp_retrans=92, link_util=1.0. The TCP goodput is far above 50% of 1 Gbps, so the scheduler must be giving TCP some or all of the UDP share that UDP does not use. The main unexplained things are: (1) the minimum weightUdp that keeps udp_loss_frac <= 0.01, (2) whether TCP goodput is essentially independent of weightUdp once UDP demand is below its configured share, and (3) whether queuePkts, tcpVariant, or duration can change TCP goodput by more than 1% while still meeting the UDP-loss condition.

body.text: UDP loss appears only when weightUdp is below the UDP demand share; the threshold for udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 lies between 0.25 and 0.50.

body.prediction: udp_loss_frac at weightUdp=0.25 is >0.01, while udp_loss_frac at weightUdp=0.50 is <=0.01.

body.observations: The ledger shows a TCP plateau: at weightUdp=0.32 through 0.50, tcp_goodput_bps is about 668.633 Mbps with udp_loss_frac=0 and link_util=1.0 (E1, E2). Lowering weightUdp below about 0.31 causes UDP loss; at 0.305 loss is 0.004622 and TCP is 669.999 Mbps, only 0.20% above the plateau, and at 0.30 loss is 0.020944 and TCP is 674.820 Mbps, only 0.93% above the plateau, so the tested TCP gains from small UDP loss are inside the 1% tolerance. TCP variants do not beat Cubic: BBR and Vegas are much lower, while NewReno, LinuxReno, and Bic are equal to Cubic within tolerance (E2, C6). duration=2 and duration=30 are equal to duration=10 (C7). The main unexplained result is queue size: queuePkts=4 gives the same TCP goodput as queuePkts=100 but many more TCP drops, while queuePkts=1000 gives zero drops but 660.830 Mbps, 1.17% lower. It is not yet known whether any intermediate queue size can raise TCP goodput by more than 1% while keeping UDP loss <=0.01, nor whether the q=1000 loss is caused by queueing delay interacting with the 1 MB TCP buffer. The next experiment therefore sweeps queue sizes and tests the weight boundary just below 0.32.

body.observations: The ledger shows a clear plateau: with TcpCubic, queuePkts=100, duration=10, tcp_goodput_bps is about 668.633 Mbps whenever weightUdp is at least about 0.31, while udp_goodput_bps is 300 Mbps and udp_loss_frac is 0. Below that, UDP loss rises: weightUdp=0.305 gives loss 0.004622 and TCP 669.999 Mbps; 0.304 gives loss 0.007888 and TCP 670.963 Mbps; 0.302 gives loss 0.014414 and TCP 672.893 Mbps; 0.30 gives loss 0.020944 and TCP 674.820 Mbps. Thus the only way to raise TCP above the plateau is to let UDP lose packets, and the feasible gain before the 1% UDP-loss limit is inside the 1% tolerance. Queue sweep at weightUdp=0.32 shows queuePkts=4 through 512 all have TCP within tolerance of 668.633 Mbps, with TCP drops decreasing as queue grows; queuePkts=1000 gives 660.830 Mbps, 1.17% lower, with zero drops. The series for r015 shows a persistent TCP queue around 946 and cwnd fixed at 1,051,248 bytes, while r008 has a much smaller queue and oscillating cwnd with periodic drops, and r014 has near-empty queues but frequent drops. TCP variants: NewReno, LinuxReno, and Bic match Cubic within tolerance; BBR and Vegas are much lower. Duration 2 and 30 match duration 10. The main remaining unexplained detail is why queuePkts=1000 lowers TCP by 1.17% with no drops, but this does not change the best setting because smaller queues are already on the plateau.

The rival predicted a >1% feasible gain from lowering weightUdp, and it did not occur.
body.next: Do not recommend a weight below the UDP-demand floor for a meaningful TCP gain; the UDP loss constraint binds before TCP can improve by more than tolerance.

body.limit: At the recommendation, TCP is limited by UDP's actual link demand and by TCP packet overhead, not by the configured UDP share, queue size, or congestion-control variant. UDP delivers 300 Mbps payload but consumes roughly 31% of the 1 Gbps wire because of packet overhead; the scheduler gives TCP the unused UDP share, so TCP payload saturates at about 668.633 Mbps with link_util=1.0. Lowering weightUdp can steal capacity from UDP, but the UDP loss constraint stops any meaningful gain: weightUdp=0.304 gives only 670.963 Mbps, 0.35% higher and inside tolerance, with udp_loss_frac=0.007888; weightUdp=0.302 gives 672.893 Mbps but violates the condition with udp_loss_frac=0.014414. Queue sizes 4-512 and loss-based TCP variants reach the same plateau, while queuePkts=1000 lowers TCP by 1.17% and BBR/Vegas underuse the link. Evidence: E0, E1, E2, E3, C1, C4, C6, C7, C8, C9, V1, V4, V6, V7.
body.explanation: The default settings lie on the TCP plateau: weightUdp=0.5 is above the UDP-demand floor, so UDP loss is zero, and the scheduler gives TCP the unused UDP share, producing the same TCP goodput as weights down to about 0.31. Since all feasible weights at or above that floor are equal within tolerance, the simplest and safest choice is the default 0.5. queuePkts=100 is also on the flat part of the queue sweep: it avoids the very high TCP retransmissions seen at queuePkts=4 and the 1.17% bufferbloat-like loss seen at queuePkts=1000. TcpCubic is tied with other loss-based variants; BBR and Vegas are worse because they do not saturate the link. duration does not affect the measured average because the system is in steady state.
body.holds_when: The UDP application remains a constant 300 Mbps source, the link remains 1 Gbps with 50 us one-way delay, the scheduler redistributes unused UDP share to TCP, TCP is always backlogged, and the default seed is used.
body.breaks_when: The recommendation would change if UDP rate or packet size changes the UDP wire-demand threshold, if the scheduler does not give unused UDP share to TCP, if the UDP loss tolerance is made much stricter or looser, if queuePkts is forced very large causing bufferbloat, or if a TCP variant that underuses the link is selected.

claims.text: The scheduler gives TCP the unused UDP share, because TCP goodput is flat at about 668.633 Mbps for weightUdp from 0.32 through 0.50 while UDP loss is zero.
The UDP loss constraint sets the practical lower bound for weightUdp near 0.31; lowering it below that gives less than a 1% TCP gain before udp_loss_frac exceeds 0.01.
Queue sizes 4 through 512, loss-based TCP variants, and durations 2, 10, and 30 do not raise TCP goodput more than 1% over the plateau; queuePkts=1000, TcpBbr, and TcpVegas lower it.

At the recommendation the link is saturated and UDP demand leaves about 69% of the wire for TCP, so TCP payload is limited by UDP's actual wire demand and packet overhead rather than by queue size or congestion control.
Very small queues increase TCP drops and retransmissions without changing goodput, while a very large queue causes persistent queueing and a measurable TCP goodput loss.

open_questions: The exact mechanism of the 1.17% TCP goodput drop at queuePkts=1000 with zero drops is not fully settled; the series suggests persistent queueing, but a direct RTT or scheduler-interaction test was not run.
The exact UDP wire-demand threshold between weightUdp=0.305 and 0.31 is inferred from loss and throughput, not directly measured from packet-level wire overhead.
Whether other seeds shift the feasible weight boundary by a small amount was not tested.
